title: Affine group points from tensor-compatible representation endomorphisms
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], let $G$ be an affine $k$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and let $R$ be a commutative $k$-algebra. For every finite-dimensional rational representation $(V,r_V)$ of $G$ [lem-sfb-rational-representation-comodule-dictionary], write $V_R=R\otimes_k V$ [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] and let $\lambda_V:V_R\to V_R$ be an $R$-linear endomorphism. Suppose that under the canonical tensor identification $(V\otimes_kW)_R\simeq V_R\otimes_RW_R$ one has $\lambda_{V\otimes W}=\lambda_V\otimes_R\lambda_W$ for every pair of representations; that $\lambda_k=\mathrm{id}_R$ on the one-dimensional trivial representation; and that $\lambda_W\circ(1\otimes u)=(1\otimes u)\circ\lambda_V$ for every $G$-equivariant $k$-linear map $u:V\to W$. Then there is a unique $g\in G(R)$ such that $r_{V,R}(g)=\lambda_V$ for every finite-dimensional rational representation $V$. No invertibility assumption on the $\lambda_V$ is needed. All vector spaces are taken in one fixed universe and their families in a containing universe.

source.place: Theorem 9.2, printed pp.164--165: recovery of an algebraic group from all finite-dimensional representations, conditions (a), (b), (c).

proof.text: We use left scalar extensions throughout; the symmetry $v\otimes a\leftrightarrow a\otimes v$ identifies these with the convention of [lem-sfb-rational-representation-comodule-dictionary]. All tensor identifications and maps below are defined on pure tensors using [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. For a finite-dimensional subspace $U\subset M$, delete dependent vectors from a finite spanning list to obtain a basis; extend it to a basis of $M$ by [lem-weil-pbc-vector-space-basis-through-vector]. Sending the extra basis vectors to zero gives $p:M\to U$ with $pi=1_U$. Hence $(1_R\otimes p)(1_R\otimes i)=1_{U_R}$: scalar extension of any such inclusion is injective for every $R$, with no assumption that $R$ is a field or a domain. The same argument applies with any other vector space in the tensor factor. Write $A=k[G]$ with the Hopf maps of [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf], and $A_R=R\otimes_kA$ with multiplication $(a\otimes f)(b\otimes h)=ab\otimes fh$ from [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property].

source.place: Theorem 9.2, pp.164--165, scalar-extension conventions; elementary basis-retraction justification for the subspace identifications.

proof.text: The coaction $\Delta:A\to A\otimes_kA$ makes $A$ a right comodule, by coassociativity and the counit identity [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf]. It therefore gives the regular rational representation by [lem-sfb-rational-representation-comodule-dictionary]. By [lem-sfb-comodule-finite-subrepresentation], every finite subset of $A$ is contained in a finite-dimensional rational subrepresentation. Moreover any two finite-dimensional subrepresentations $U,W$ lie in a third one $Z$: apply that statement to the union of finite spanning lists for $U$ and $W$. Every inclusion here is equivariant by the dictionary's criterion for intertwining maps. Thus condition (c) of the item applies to their scalar extensions.

source.place: Chapter 4(d), p.87, regular representation; Corollary 4.8, p.86; Theorem 9.2, first proof paragraph.

proof.text: For $f\in A$ choose a finite subrepresentation $U$ containing it, with inclusion $i_U:U\to A$, and define $l(f)=(1_R\otimes i_U)\lambda_U(1\otimes f)\in A_R$. This is independent of $U$: for another choice $W$, choose $Z$ as in Step 2 and apply condition (c) to $U\hookrightarrow Z$ and $W\hookrightarrow Z$. Both expressions become $(1_R\otimes i_Z)\lambda_Z(1\otimes f)$. To check $k$-linearity choose one such $Z$ containing the finitely many vectors involved; linearity is then that of $\lambda_Z$ and $1_R\otimes i_Z$. By [lem-weil-pbc-module-base-change-universal-property], $l$ extends uniquely to an $R$-linear map $L:A_R\to A_R$, $L(a\otimes f)=a\,l(f)$. Its restriction satisfies $L(1_R\otimes i_U)=(1_R\otimes i_U)\lambda_U$ for every finite subrepresentation $U$, since the two sides agree on every $1\otimes f$. These tensors generate by [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product].

source.place: Theorem 9.2, pp.164--165, extension from finite-dimensional subrepresentations, specialized to the regular representation.

proof.text: Let $U,W\subset A$ be finite subrepresentations. Choose finite spanning lists $(u_i)$ and $(w_j)$, and by [lem-sfb-comodule-finite-subrepresentation] choose a finite subrepresentation $Z\subset A$ containing all products $u_iw_j$. Bilinearity gives a map $m:U\otimes_kW\to Z$, $u\otimes w\mapsto uw$. Its domain is finite-dimensional: the finitely many $u_i\otimes w_j$ span by the tensor universal property. This map is equivariant. Indeed the tensor coaction in [lem-sfb-rational-representation-comodule-dictionary] gives $u\otimes w\mapsto\sum(u_{(1)}\otimes w_{(1)})\otimes u_{(2)}w_{(2)}$, while the coaction of the product is $\Delta(uw)=\Delta(u)\Delta(w)=\sum u_{(1)}w_{(1)}\otimes u_{(2)}w_{(2)}$, by [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf]. These are the same after $m\otimes1$. Equality in $Z\otimes_kA$ follows from equality in $A\otimes_kA$ by the split inclusion of Step 1. The dictionary now gives equivariance of $m$.

source.place: Theorem 9.2, p.165, equivariance of multiplication and its footnote, with the finite-dimensional range made explicit.

proof.text:
For $f\in U$, $h\in W$, condition (c) for $m$ in Step 4 and condition (a) give
$$L(1\otimes fh)=m_R\bigl(\lambda_U(1\otimes f)\otimes_R\lambda_W(1\otimes h)\bigr)=L(1\otimes f)L(1\otimes h),$$
where $m_R$ is followed by $Z_R\to A_R$. Here we use the canonical scalar tensor identification assumed in the statement. By $R$-linearity and distributivity this identity holds for arbitrary finite sums of pure tensors, hence $L(xy)=L(x)L(y)$ for all $x,y\in A_R$. Choose a finite subrepresentation $U$ containing $1_A$. The map $k\to U$, $a\mapsto a1_A$, is equivariant because $\Delta(1_A)=1_A\otimes1_A$ [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf, lem-sfb-rational-representation-comodule-dictionary]. Conditions (b),(c) for this map give $L(1_R\otimes1_A)=1_R\otimes1_A$. Thus $L$ is a unital $R$-algebra endomorphism of $A_R$, using the multiplication of [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property].

source.place: Theorem 9.2, p.165, algebra-homomorphism consequence of multiplication equivariance and conditions (a)--(c).

proof.text:
The map $\epsilon_R:A_R\to R$, $a\otimes f\mapsto a\epsilon(f)$, is an $R$-algebra map: $\epsilon$ preserves products and unit by [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf], so [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property] applies to the maps $R\to R$ and $A\xrightarrow{\epsilon}k\to R$. Therefore
$$g^*:A\longrightarrow R,\qquad f\longmapsto\epsilon_R L(1\otimes f)$$
is a $k$-algebra homomorphism, as a composite of unital algebra maps (Step 5). It defines $g\in G(R)$ by [def-weil-affine-spectrum], equivalently by the explicit $G(R)=\operatorname{Hom}_{k\text{-alg}}(A,R)$ convention in [lem-sfb-rational-representation-comodule-dictionary]. This is extraction of the value at the identity in the regular-representation argument; no inverse of $L$ has been used.

source.place: Lemma 9.1, p.164, extraction of the value at the identity; Theorem 9.2, p.165. The comparison with other representations is checked by coefficient maps in Steps 7--9.

proof.text:
Fix a finite-dimensional representation $V$ with coaction $c_V:V\to V\otimes_kA$ and a $k$-linear functional $\phi:V\to k$. Define its coefficient map $f_\phi=(\phi\otimes1)c_V:V\to A$. Coassociativity from [lem-sfb-rational-representation-comodule-dictionary], after applying $\phi$ to the first vector-space factor, gives
$$\Delta f_\phi=(f_\phi\otimes1)c_V.$$
Thus $f_\phi$ is equivariant into the regular representation, by the intertwining criterion of the same node. The counit identity gives $\epsilon f_\phi=\phi$. Both are equalities of linear maps, obtained by applying the displayed tensor maps to the comodule identities; they are not conclusions from testing $k$-valued points.

source.place: Proposition 4.12, p.88, coassociativity and counit argument for the coaction embedding; Theorem 9.2, p.165, last comparison paragraph. Its components are written as coefficient maps.

proof.text:
Choose a finite spanning list $(v_i)$ of $V$. The finite-subrepresentation theorem [lem-sfb-comodule-finite-subrepresentation] supplies $U\subset A$ containing every $f_\phi(v_i)$, hence the whole image of $f_\phi$. The factorization $q:V\to U$ is equivariant: compose its proposed coaction equality with $U\otimes_kA\hookrightarrow A\otimes_kA$, use Step 7, and cancel the split inclusion of Step 1. Consequently condition (c) gives $\lambda_Uq_R=q_R\lambda_V$. Combining this with the defining restriction of $L$ in Step 3 gives
$$L(f_\phi)_R=(f_\phi)_R\lambda_V.$$
Applying $\epsilon_R$ and using $\epsilon f_\phi=\phi$ yields
$$\epsilon_R L(f_\phi)_R=\phi_R\lambda_V,$$
where $\phi_R(a\otimes v)=a\phi(v)$. All scalar-extended maps here are furnished by [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product].

source.place: Theorem 9.2, p.165, comparison through the coaction embedding; finite-dimensional factorization of each coefficient map.

proof.text:
Write $c_V(v)=\sum_i v_i\otimes a_i$. The point-action formula of [lem-sfb-rational-representation-comodule-dictionary] gives
$$\phi_R r_{V,R}(g)(1\otimes v)=\sum_i\phi(v_i)g^*(a_i)=g^*(f_\phi(v))=\epsilon_R L(1\otimes f_\phi(v))=\phi_R\lambda_V(1\otimes v),$$
the last equality being Step 8. For a finite basis $(e_j)$ of $V$, take $\phi$ successively to be its coordinate functionals. They detect equality on $R\otimes_kV$: the mutually inverse maps $(b_j)\mapsto\sum_jb_j\otimes e_j$ and $x\mapsto(\phi_{j,R}(x))_j$ are inverse on pure tensors by [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. Thus $r_{V,R}(g)$ and $\lambda_V$ agree on $1\otimes v$, and by $R$-linearity on all of $V_R$. A finite basis is obtained by deleting dependent vectors from a finite spanning list [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace]. If $V=0$, the same argument has an empty basis and both operators are the unique endomorphism of zero.

source.place: Theorem 9.2, p.165, equality on every finite-dimensional representation, with the coordinate calculation of Proposition 4.12 made explicit.

proof.text:
For uniqueness suppose $h\in G(R)$ has the prescribed actions. The dictionary [lem-sfb-rational-representation-comodule-dictionary] defines its action $r_{A,R}(h)$ on the possibly infinite-dimensional regular representation. For every finite subrepresentation $U\subset A$, equivariance of inclusion gives $r_{A,R}(h)(1_R\otimes i_U)=(1_R\otimes i_U)r_{U,R}(h)=(1_R\otimes i_U)\lambda_U$. Every $f\in A$ lies in such a $U$ (Step 2), so this equality and pure-tensor generation give $r_{A,R}(h)=L$. If $\Delta(f)=\sum f_{(1)}\otimes f_{(2)}$, the dictionary and counit give
$$\epsilon_Rr_{A,R}(h)(1\otimes f)=\sum\epsilon(f_{(1)})h^*(f_{(2)})=h^*(f).$$
Consequently $h^*(f)=\epsilon_RL(1\otimes f)=g^*(f)$ for every $f$, hence $h=g$ by [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. This uses neither a chosen faithful finite representation nor an invertibility assumption on any $\lambda_V$. Finally each $\lambda_V=r_{V,R}(g)$ is automatically invertible, with inverse $r_{V,R}(g^{-1})$, since the dictionary supplies a group homomorphism.

source.place: Theorem 9.2, p.165, uniqueness; Lemma 9.1, p.164, evaluation at the identity; Note 9.3 for automatic invertibility.

proof_origin.place: Theorem 9.2 and Lemma 9.1, printed pp.164--165, using Corollary 4.8 and Proposition 4.12 (pp.86,88). The coaction comparison is expanded into coefficient maps; uniqueness is extracted by the counit instead of choosing a faithful representation.
